Reading a certificate

Source: vignettes/certificates.Rmd
certificates.Rmd

Installation 

install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("gcol33/linop")

Installing linop installs one package. There are no Imports and no compiled code, so there is no toolchain to have working first. Matrix sits in Suggests and is used for sparse leaves and as_sparse().

R 4.4.0 or newer. The floor is set by crossprod() and tcrossprod(), which became S3 generic in R 4.4.0, and are what let one matrixOps method cover all three matrix products.

One object, five shapes

Every computation in this package that could be wrong comes back with a certificate. It is the same class each time, and it takes five shapes, because the questions differ:

produced_by subject
verify() does the operator behave like a linear map
solve(), square how close is x to solving A x = b
solve(), least squares how close is x to minimising ||b - A x||
eigs(), svds() how close is (theta, x) to an eigenpair
eigs() on a sequence space how close is theta to the spectrum of the operator that was truncated

This article is about the last four. verify() is covered in vignette("adapters"), where it belongs to the job of writing an operator.

Getting hold of one

Each verb puts its certificate where its own return value has room. A solve returns the solution a matrix solve would return and carries the certificate in an attribute; the spectral verbs return a result object with a field; verify() returns the certificate itself. certificate() reads it off any of them.

n <- 200
lap <- function(X) 2 * X - rbind(X[-1, , drop = FALSE], 0) - rbind(0, X[-n, , drop = FALSE])
L <- linop(lap, adjoint = lap, dim = c(n, n), properties = c(hermitian = TRUE))
b <- as.numeric(L %*% sin(seq_len(n) * pi / (n + 1)))

cert <- certificate(solve(L, b, method = "minres", tol = 1e-10))
cert
#> solved by minres (named by the caller, so no evidence minimum was applied)
#> ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
#> check                          status       source           guarantee             conf
#> ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
#> arithmetic floor               pass         computation      estimate              -
#> residual                       pass         computation      identity              1
#> backward error                 pass         computation      estimate              -
#> convergence                    pass         computation      identity              1
#> forward error                  not_checked  computation      identity              -
#> ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
#> overall                        qualified   no deterministic bound on: arithmetic floor, backward error, forward error

A certificate belongs to a result rather than to an operator. An operator on its own has nothing to certify: the one claim it can make alone is that it satisfies the contract, and that is verify(), which returns a certificate of its own.

The attribute on a solve survives arithmetic and is dropped by indexing, as.numeric(), c() and the reductions. So the cost of solve() returning a plain matrix is not that the certificate is easily lost; it is that 2 * x still carries one describing x.

Status and evidence are separate questions

Every row of that table carries a status and, separately, the kind of argument behind it.

The status column answers whether the check passed. pass, fail, not_checked, and qualified, which means it passed for a reason weaker than the clean one.

The three columns after it are the evidence, and they are three independent fields rather than a ranking. source is what kind of argument produced the number: a computation on data at hand, a theorem, a construction, a user_declaration. guarantee is what the argument gives you: an identity holds exactly, a deterministic_bound holds always, an estimate holds usually. confidence is a probability where one applies and - where none does.

A pass behind an estimate and a pass behind an identity are both passes and they are not the same claim. The summary line names the rows with neither kind of deterministic guarantee, so that distinction survives being skimmed:

cert$without_deterministic_bound
#> [1] "arithmetic floor" "backward error"   "forward error"

The rows of a linear solve

row measures
arithmetic floor the level below which no residual is meaningful
residual ||b - A x|| / ||b||
backward error ||r|| / (||A|| ||x|| + ||b||), the Rigal-Gaches quantity
convergence whether the iteration stopped because it was done
forward error how far x is from the true solution

The backward error is the row to read. It answers a question that has an exact answer: it is the size of the smallest perturbation to A and b for which your computed x is the exact solution. A backward error of 1e-14 means you solved a problem within 1e-14 of the one you asked about.

||A|| in that denominator is a lower bound rather than an estimate in either direction, deliberately. Shrinking the denominator can only make the reported backward error larger, so the number can overstate the error and never understate it.

The arithmetic floor

Ask for an exact solve and no floating-point iteration can deliver it:

tight <- solve(L, b, method = "minres", tol = 0, maxit = 400)
bare  <- solve(L, b, method = "minres", tol = 0, maxit = 400,
               control = list(floor_const = 0))

identical(as.numeric(tight), as.numeric(bare))
#> [1] TRUE

The same iteration ran twice and produced the same vector, bit for bit. Only the certificates differ:

c(with_floor = attr(tight, "certificate")$overall,
  without    = attr(bare,  "certificate")$overall)
#>  with_floor     without 
#> "qualified"      "fail"
attr(bare, "certificate")
#> solved by minres (named by the caller, so no evidence minimum was applied)
#> ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
#> check                          status       source           guarantee             conf
#> ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
#> arithmetic floor               pass         computation      estimate              -
#> residual                       fail         computation      estimate              -
#> backward error                 fail         computation      estimate              -
#> convergence                    fail         computation      identity              1
#> forward error                  not_checked  computation      identity              -
#> ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
#> overall                        fail   no deterministic bound on: arithmetic floor, residual, backward error, forward error
#> 
#> failures:
#>   residual: worst ||b - A x|| / ||b|| = 9.961e-13 against tol 0.000e+00, floor 0.000e+00
#>   backward error: worst ||r|| / (||A|| ||x|| + ||b||) = 6.084e-17 against tol 0.000e+00
#>   convergence: 400 of at most 400 iterations; budget exhausted

A backward error of 1.8e-16 is reported as a failure, because it was tested against a tolerance of zero with nothing underneath it. The floor is what stops a fully converged solve from certifying as fail, and it is c * eps * (||A|| ||x|| + ||b||), which is Higham’s bound on the computed residual. That is the same quantity as the Rigal-Gaches denominator, so once the backward error is written relatively the floor is a plain c * eps.

A row that meets its tolerance only because of the floor says qualified and carries an estimate, never a clean identity. c counts terms in an inner product a matrix-free operator never exposes, so it is an argument with a default rather than a constant.

The same table, measured differently

A least-squares solve has no exact answer. b - A x does not go to zero, so testing it against a tolerance would report a converged solution as a failure. What goes to zero is A^H r.

Both are backward errors, so one row carries both readings, and which one applies is decided by measurement rather than by the method that was called:

G <- matrix(rnorm(120 * 40), 120, 40)
R <- linop(G)

incompatible <- solve(R, rnorm(120), method = "lsmr", tol = 1e-10)
compatible   <- solve(R, as.numeric(G %*% rnorm(40)), method = "lsmr", tol = 1e-10)

status_of <- function(x, row) {
  ch <- attr(x, "certificate")$checks
  ch$status[ch$check == row]
}
c(incompatible = status_of(incompatible, "residual"),
  compatible   = status_of(compatible,   "residual"))
#>  incompatible    compatible 
#> "not_checked"        "pass"

For the incompatible right-hand side the residual reads not_checked, because it has a nonzero minimum and comparing that to tol would mean nothing. For the compatible one the same code found a residual that did go to zero and checked it.

attr(incompatible, "certificate")
#> solved by lsmr (named by the caller, so no evidence minimum was applied)
#> ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
#> check                          status       source           guarantee             conf
#> ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
#> arithmetic floor               pass         computation      identity              1
#> residual                       not_checked  computation      estimate              -
#> backward error                 pass         computation      identity              1
#> convergence                    pass         computation      identity              1
#> forward error                  not_checked  computation      identity              -
#> ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
#> overall                        qualified   no deterministic bound on: residual, forward error

The perturbation behind the least-squares reading is Stewart’s, dA = -(r r^H A) / ||r||^2, which is exhibited rather than argued: it is an actual matrix of that norm making x an exact minimiser. That is what makes ||A^H r|| / (||A|| ||r||) a backward error rather than a heuristic, and it is also Paige and Saunders’ stopping rule.

A third shape, for an eigenpair

For a solve, b is data and A is data, and the Rigal-Gaches denominator has a term for each. For an eigenpair, theta and x are both outputs and A is the only datum, so the denominator loses a term and the table gains rows:

fit <- eigs(L, k = 3, which = "largest_algebraic", ncv = 60)
fit$certificate
#> solved by primme (hermitian operator, PRIMME with implicit restarting (highest priority))
#> ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
#> check                          status       source           guarantee             conf
#> ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
#> arithmetic floor               pass         computation      estimate              -
#> residual                       pass         computation      identity              1
#> orthogonality                  pass         computation      identity              1
#> backward error                 pass         computation      estimate              -
#> target identity                not_checked  computation      identity              -
#> convergence                    pass         computation      identity              1
#> forward error                  pass         theorem          deterministic_bound   1
#> ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
#> overall                        qualified   no deterministic bound on: arithmetic floor, backward error, target identity

orthogonality is new: the computed vectors should be orthonormal, and this measures whether they are. target identity is new and is always not_checked, which is the honest entry. A small residual proves the pair is an approximate eigenpair. That it is the largest one needs an inertia count, an enclosure or a separation bound, and matrix-free there is generally none available.

The one row that is sometimes a bound

forward error is not_checked on every linear solve in this article, and it is not laziness. Nothing constrains it. At a condition number of 1e10:

m <- 40
Q <- qr.Q(qr(matrix(rnorm(m * m), m, m)))
M <- Q %*% diag(10^seq(0, -10, length.out = m)) %*% t(Q)
M <- (M + t(M)) / 2
Aill <- linop(M)
xtrue <- rnorm(m)
bill <- as.numeric(Aill %*% xtrue)

t(vapply(c("minres", "gmres", "bicgstab"), function(mth) {
  z <- solve(Aill, bill, method = mth, tol = 1e-10, maxit = 400)
  c(backward = attr(z, "certificate")$values$backward_error,
    forward  = max(abs(z - xtrue)) / max(abs(xtrue)))
}, numeric(2)))
#>              backward   forward
#> minres   6.433681e-11 0.3207462
#> gmres    4.258965e-11 0.2493074
#> bicgstab 2.537527e-09 0.6736162

Backward errors around 1e-11 sit beside true forward errors around 1e-1. Both columns are correct. kappa^2 * eps is 2.2e4 here, and no backward error constrains the forward one at that conditioning, which is exactly why the row refuses to report a number it cannot stand behind. Do not read that spread as one method being more accurate than another.

For an eigenpair the same row does carry a bound, and it is the first in the package. A + E with E = -r x^H - x r^H is hermitian and has theta as an exact eigenvalue, so Weyl’s inequality gives min_j |theta - lambda_j(A)| <= ||r|| / ||x||:

fwd <- fit$certificate$checks
fwd <- fwd[fwd$check == "forward error", ]
fwd[, c("status", "source", "guarantee")]
#>   status  source           guarantee
#> 7   pass theorem deterministic_bound
cat(fwd$detail)
#> min_j |theta - lambda_j(A)| <= 3.969e-10, that is 9.924e-11 relative to ||A||; the eigenvectors are not covered, which needs a certified separation and not a Ritz gap

source is theorem and guarantee is deterministic_bound, the only row of this shape where either appears. The bound is about some eigenvalue of A; which one is the target identity question and stays not_checked.

Evidence can carry a dependency

That bound holds because A is hermitian. If the only argument for that is your say-so, the bound inherits it, and the certificate records the inheritance rather than hiding it:

Md <- crossprod(matrix(rnorm(20 * 20), 20, 20)) + diag(20)

checked  <- eigs(linop(Md), k = 2, which = "largest_algebraic")
declared <- eigs(linop(function(X) Md %*% X, adjoint = function(X) Md %*% X,
                       dim = c(20, 20), properties = c(hermitian = TRUE)),
                 k = 2, which = "largest_algebraic")

checked$certificate$evidence[["forward error"]]
#> theorem / deterministic_bound / conf 1 <- [computation / identity / conf 1]
declared$certificate$evidence[["forward error"]]
#> theorem / deterministic_bound / conf 1 <- [user_declaration / identity / conf 1]

Both say theorem / deterministic_bound. What differs is in the brackets, and it is what a requirement tests:

strict <- requirement(sources = c("construction", "computation", "theorem"),
                      guarantees = c("identity", "deterministic_bound"))

c(checked  = evidence_satisfies(checked$certificate$evidence[["forward error"]],  strict),
  declared = evidence_satisfies(declared$certificate$evidence[["forward error"]], strict))
#>  checked declared 
#>     TRUE    FALSE

A theorem applied to a declaration is worth what the declaration is worth. This is the same rule that stops a sum of two declared positive-definite operators from satisfying CG’s requirement, described in vignette("capabilities"), reaching the certificate.

A fifth shape, about an operator that is not there

Every shape so far certifies a computation against the operator the computation ran on. A finite section certifies a statement about the operator it truncated, which no computation touched:

H <- linop_jacobi(diagonal = 1)
dim(H)
#> [1] Inf Inf

fit <- eigs(H, k = 1, which = "largest_algebraic")
certificate(fit)
#> solved by primme on a finite section (operator on l^2(Z); width 41 -> 49, stopped because the tail is below half the tolerance)
#> ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
#> check                          status       source           guarantee             conf
#> ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
#> arithmetic floor               pass         construction     deterministic_bound   1
#> finite residual                pass         computation      identity              1
#> orthogonality                  pass         computation      identity              1
#> truncation bound               pass         theorem          deterministic_bound   1
#> isolation                      pass         theorem          deterministic_bound   1
#> enclosure                      pass         theorem          estimate              -
#> convergence                    pass         computation      identity              1
#> forward error                  pass         theorem          deterministic_bound   1
#> ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
#> overall                        pass   no deterministic bound on: enclosure

The width was not given either. eigs() on an operator with no matrix truncates it, and the header records which widths it went through and why it stopped; vignette("sequence-spaces") covers how that width is chosen.

residual and backward error are gone, because a truncated eigenvalue answers no equation with data in it. What replaces them is a split, and the split is the point:

v <- fit$certificate$values
c(finite_residual = v$residual, truncation = v$truncation, bound = v$bound)
#> finite_residual      truncation           bound 
#>    1.653582e-10    5.313083e-11    1.736869e-10

The residual of the extended eigenvector against the infinite operator is those two terms in quadrature, exactly. The first is what the eigensolve left behind and answers to tol and ncv; the second is what the truncation costs and answers to n. Reported as one number you would know the size of the error without knowing which knob moves it:

narrow <- eigs(finite_section(H, n = 12), k = 1, which = "largest_algebraic")
nv <- narrow$certificate$values
c(finite_residual = nv$residual, truncation = nv$truncation)
#> finite_residual      truncation 
#>    7.913351e-11    1.815373e-03

At n = 12 the eigensolve is four orders better than it needs to be and the section is six orders short, and the convergence row says which:

ch <- narrow$certificate$checks
cat(ch$detail[ch$check == "convergence"])
#> 0 of 1 requested pairs converged in 33 of at most 500 iterations; the eigensolve met its target and the section did not; the truncation term is 1.815e-03 at n = 12

isolation is the row with no counterpart anywhere else. The essential spectrum of this class is known exactly rather than estimated, so a value can be tested against it, and a value that has not cleared it is a discretisation of continuous spectrum rather than an eigenvalue:

free <- eigs(finite_section(linop_jacobi(diagonal = 0), n = 100), k = 1,
             which = "largest_algebraic")
free$values
#> [1] 1.999758
free$certificate$checks[, c("check", "status")]
#>              check      status
#> 1 arithmetic floor        pass
#> 2  finite residual        pass
#> 3    orthogonality        pass
#> 4 truncation bound        fail
#> 5        isolation        fail
#> 6        enclosure not_checked
#> 7      convergence        fail
#> 8    forward error        fail

The operator with no potential has no eigenvalues at all. The eigensolver does not notice: it converges cleanly and hands back a number just inside the band. Only the isolation row separates no eigenvalue here from a hard eigenvalue here, and it is what makes the whole certificate refuse.

The forward error row here rests on nothing declared. The class is self-adjoint by construction and the residual identity is arithmetic, so unlike the eigenpair version it carries no dependency at all:

fit$certificate$evidence[["forward error"]]
#> theorem / deterministic_bound / conf 1

Reading one in code

The printed table is for people. The object is a list, so a package can test against it:

names(cert)
#> [1] "subject"                     "checks"                     
#> [3] "overall"                     "without_deterministic_bound"
#> [5] "probes"                      "values"                     
#> [7] "evidence"                    "dispatch"
cert$checks[, c("check", "status")]
#>              check      status
#> 1 arithmetic floor        pass
#> 2         residual        pass
#> 3   backward error        pass
#> 4      convergence        pass
#> 5    forward error not_checked
cert$values$backward_error
#> [1] 4.895612e-15
stopifnot(cert$overall %in% c("pass", "qualified"))

cert$dispatch records which method ran and why, cert$values holds the measured quantities, and cert$evidence holds the evidence objects for rows that carry a dependency.
